papers.title_in_file: Robustness of quantum algorithms against coherent control errors
papers.version_note: arXiv:2303.00618v3, dated December 4, 2024; the file name says 2023.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that bounds the worst-case fidelity loss of quantum circuits under coherent control errors using Lipschitz bounds based on Hamiltonian norms, with a 3-qubit QFT gate-set simulation, an ibm nairobi experiment and a variational-circuit regularization example.

existing.value: The authors state that the Lipschitz bound (17) is in general not tight, since the coupling between sequentially applied gates is not taken into account.
quotes: It is important to note that the Lipschitz bound (17) itself is, in general, not tight, e.g., since the coupling between sequentially applied gates is not taken into account.
existing.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their bound in Section II B.

existing.value: The authors derive worst-case fidelity bounds which show that resilience against coherent control errors is mainly influenced by the norms of the Hamiltonians generating the individual gates.
existing.anchor: Abstract, p.1; Theorem II.2, Section II B, p.4
quotes: We derive worst-case fidelity bounds which show that the resilience against coherent control errors is mainly influenced by the norms of the Hamiltonians generating the individual gates.
Thus, smaller norms ∥Hi∥2 imply better robustness against such errors.
existing.certainty_reason: Theorem II.2 is proved in Appendix A; the bound is an upper bound on fidelity loss.
existing.reader_inference: The result is about an upper bound on the loss; the paper says the bound is in general not tight, so a smaller bound does not by itself guarantee a smaller true loss.

existing.note: Supported by the paper only as a comparison of five transpiled circuits in simulation. The text gives the gate-count example (gate set C against gate set E) and says a similar observation holds for depth; the gate-set comparison does not claim any gate set is generally better.
existing.value: The authors report that, using the 3-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform as an example, the guideline of reducing Hamiltonian norms targets robustness more effectively than existing guidelines based on circuit depth or gate count.
quotes: Using the 3-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform as an example application, we demonstrate that this guideline targets robustness more effectively than existing ones based on circuit depth or gate count.
A similar observation can be made when comparing the circuit depths.
existing.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulation study of five transpiled circuits.
existing.reader_inference: Five circuits from one transpiler (BQSKit); the depth comparison is stated without numbers in the text (the figure holds them).

assertions.value: The authors define a coherent control error as a perturbation of an ideal gate in which the generating Hamiltonian is multiplied by one plus an unknown real noise term, which may be stochastic or time-varying.
quotes: Mathematically, a coherent control error can be described as a perturbation
of an ideal quantum gate e−iH , where H = H† is the Hamiltonian generating the gate. Further, ε ∈ R is an unknown, possibly stochastic and/or time-varying noise term.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of its error model, Section I.

assertions.value: The authors state that the only assumption on the noise is a bound on its infinity norm; the errors need not be identical and the bound need not be small.
quotes: Throughout the paper, we assume that the size of the noise is bounded by some scalar ε¯ > 0, i.e., |εi| ≤ ε¯ for i = 1, . . . , N or, equivalently, ∥ε∥∞ ≤ ε¯. Beyond the existence of such a bound, we make no further assumptions.
In particular, we do not assume that the errors are identical
or that the bound ε¯ is sufficiently small
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own assumptions in Section II.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results allow independent noise terms on the gates, arbitrary unitaries defining the gates, and no assumption on the nature of the noise, such as being small or drawn from a specific distribution.
quotes: The presented results are applicable under rather general conditions: We allow for independent noise terms affecting the gates, for arbitrary unitaries defining the gates,
we do not require any assumptions on the nature of the noise, e.g., being sufficiently small or drawn from a specific probability distribution.

assertions.value: The paper states, citing Aharonov and Ben-Or, that fault-tolerant quantum computation requires the diamond distance of an error from the identity to be at most some sufficiently small positive number.
